questions.title: Water security and rural incomes in Morocco
questions.stem:
Text A — Competing uses. Repeated drought has made the reliability of Morocco's water supply an economic issue for cities and farms. The national response includes better irrigation management and additional supply. In the practice district below, groundwater is accessible to several growers: withdrawing water leaves less for neighbours, while monitoring each well is expensive. A posted charge currently applies to metered withdrawals only.

Text B — Who can adjust? Large orchards have credit and can buy drip equipment. Some tenant farmers hold one-season leases and cannot borrow against the land. Water-saving equipment can reduce withdrawals per hectare, but profitable orchards may expand planted area. A proposed charge would fund meters and a household connection grant. The alternative is a uniform subsidy on drip equipment. The treasury can fund only one new programme this year.

Text C — A pilot. The authority tested a higher charge on the same group of metered farms. Rainfall and crop prices were approximately unchanged. The neighbouring unmetered district was not in the trial. All district quantities and prices below are constructed for this exercise.

| Pilot measure | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water charge (dirhams per m³) | 1.20 | 1.50 |
| Metered withdrawals (million m³ per season) | 40 | 36 |
| Hectares planted in the pilot | 10000 | 10500 |

Background reading: World Bank, Morocco water security and resilience programme (2023). All district or scenario data and policy proposals are constructed for this paper.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Define a common pool resource in the context of the aquifer in Text A.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Define opportunity cost as it applies to the treasury's choice in Text B.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage change in metered withdrawals and the percentage change in the water charge, using initial values.

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the revenue collected from the after-pilot charge, assuming all metered withdrawals are billed and paid.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how a per-unit abstraction charge paid by growers could affect the supply of orchard fruit.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why credit constraints may cause a uniform equipment subsidy to benefit owners of large orchards more than tenant farmers.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using a production possibilities diagram, explain how a lasting deterioration in reliable water supply can change the attainable combination of farm and other output.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why a reduction in water used per hectare may fail to reduce total withdrawals in the long run.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Using the texts, data and your knowledge of economics, evaluate whether Morocco's practice district should prioritise a metered abstraction charge or an equipment subsidy to protect groundwater and rural livelihoods.

steps.text: Consumption is rival: extraction leaves less available to others (1). Exclusion of potential users is difficult or costly (1). An example alone does not establish both characteristics.
The value or benefit of the next best alternative (1) sacrificed by making a choice (1). Here it may be the benefits forgone from the other water programme.
Withdrawal change = (36 − 40)/40 × 100 = −10%. Charge change = (1.50 − 1.20)/1.20 × 100 = +25%. Award one mark for valid substitution and one for each signed result or clearly stated direction.
36 million m³ × 1.50 dirhams/m³ (1) = 54 million dirhams per season (1). Revenue is not net social benefit.

Use fruit price and fruit quantity axes. Label initial demand and supply and the new supply curve to the left or above the original (up to 2). Water is an input; the charge raises marginal costs. At unchanged demand the fruit price rises and equilibrium output falls, other things equal (up to 2).

The subsidy lowers the private purchase cost, but the grower must finance the remainder. Large growers can borrow or use retained funds. A short lease limits a tenant's time to recover the investment. Relative uptake and total subsidy received can therefore be greater for established owners. Award up to four for a linked explanation grounded in Text B.

Label farm output and other output; draw an initial frontier and a new frontier inward, particularly on the farm-output intercept if agriculture relies more heavily on water (up to 2). Lost productive capacity reduces feasible combinations; distinguish a new frontier from movement caused by temporary underuse (up to 2).

Total use equals water per hectare times area. Cheaper effective irrigation can raise returns and encourage expansion. The trial area grew from 10,000 to 10,500 hectares although total metered use fell. Continued expansion or diversion to unmetered wells could offset technical savings. Four marks for mechanism, application and a conditional conclusion.

Charging raises the marginal cost of an additional withdrawal. The pilot's 25% price rise was associated with 10% less metered water: some demand responded, but the smaller quantity response means the burden on users remains material. The 54 million dirhams collected could fund meters and connections, subject to installation and collection costs.

Subsidised drip equipment may preserve yields for each unit of water without an immediate income shock. One-season tenants might be unable to afford even the subsidised price. Cheaper irrigation can expand acreage, and charging only metered users can instead move pumping to unmetered wells. A before/after pilot with similar rainfall does not identify the nationwide response.

Prioritise metering and a charge in areas where coverage can be enforced, with grants targeted to vulnerable households. A subsidy may be the better initial policy where monitoring is infeasible and assistance reaches tenants. Compare aquifer levels, total withdrawals and farm income over several seasons before scaling up.
The illustrative metering rates are 38% for small farms, 64% for medium farms and 89% for large farms. Unequal coverage means the pilot cannot stand in for all withdrawals.

Best fit, 0–15. 0: no relevant economics. 1–3: assertions or isolated concepts. 4–6: some relevant explanation, limited application. 7–9: coherent analysis with some application and consideration of consequences. 10–12: developed, applied analysis weighing competing considerations with a supported view. 13–15: precise theory and relevant diagrams where useful, evidence integrated throughout, and a balanced judgement that explains conditions or relative importance. Other defensible conclusions can receive full credit.

questions.title: Chile and a copper revenue shock
questions.stem:
Text A — A volatile tax base. Copper is an important export for Chile. Its fiscal framework and stabilisation funds illustrate how spending can be separated from temporary commodity revenue. In this constructed budget exercise, a lower world copper price reduces profits and royalties. A mining town reports fewer orders for transport and repair work while its stock of machinery is largely unchanged.

Text B — Three pressures on the budget. A finance committee can draw on savings to maintain school repairs or postpone the work for a year. The repair contracts employ local workers, although equipment is imported. A separate proposal would fund skills training for workers moving into non-mining industries. Training takes two years and vacancies are concentrated away from the town. The treasury cannot fund every commitment indefinitely.

Text C — A price-taker. The export office assumes that shipment volume below was fixed under contract for this year. Only a fraction of export receipts enters the public budget. Its operating spending forecast was prepared before the price fall. The figures are illustrative, not reported Chilean accounts.

| Annual indicator | Baseline | Shock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copper price (US dollars per tonne) | 8400 | 7000 |
| Exports (million tonnes) | 4.0 | 4.0 |
| Public revenue (billion US dollars) | 80 | 75 |
| Public expenditure (billion US dollars) | 82 | 82 |
| Population (million) | 20 | 20 |

Background reading: IMF, Fiscal Considerations in Managing Stabilization Funds in Chile (2023). All district or scenario data and policy proposals are constructed for this paper.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate copper export revenue in each scenario and the change, in billions of US dollars.

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the shock-year budget deficit per resident.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using an AD–AS diagram, explain how the loss of export receipts could reduce real output in the short run.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why the fall in government revenue need not equal the fall in copper export revenue.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using a labour market diagram for local repair workers, explain a possible effect of postponing school repairs.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why improving occupational mobility may be insufficient to secure employment for the mining town's displaced workers.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Using the texts, data and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the use of a stabilisation fund to maintain public spending after the fall in the copper price.

steps.text: A good or service supplied by a resident of one economy (1) to a non-resident/overseas buyer (1). A transfer of money alone does not define an export.
Government expenditure exceeds government revenue (1) during a given period (1). Distinguish the annual flow from outstanding public debt.
Baseline: 8,400 × 4.0 million = US$33.60 billion (1). Shock: 7,000 × 4.0 million = US$28.00 billion (1). Revenue falls by US$5.60 billion (1).
(82 − 75) billion / 20 million (1) = US$350 per resident for the year (1). This average is not a tax bill for each individual.

Label price level and real GDP, SRAS and AD; shift AD left and indicate lower equilibrium output (up to 2). Lower net exports cut expenditure; weaker incomes and local orders can depress spending further. Assume spare capacity and other spending unchanged (up to 2).

Export revenue accrues initially to producers. Royalties and taxes capture only portions, sometimes on profit rather than total sales. Other taxes or non-mining activity can change. Here public revenue falls US$5 billion while copper receipts fall US$5.6 billion; neither number gives the royalty rate. Reward a complete mechanism with evidence.

Label wage and labour employed, labour supply and derived demand. Shift labour demand left with lower equilibrium employment (up to 2). Fewer contracts reduce the extra revenue from employing workers; wages may fall, or sticky wages may instead increase unemployment (up to 2).

Training changes the tasks workers can perform. Jobs may still be in distant towns with high moving or housing costs. Training takes two years and income is needed now. If demand is weak across industries, qualified workers can remain unemployed. Reward a linked explanation of at least one distinct remaining constraint.

With fixed volume, US$5.6 billion of copper receipts disappears. Saving in a boom and drawing down during a temporary fall can prevent simultaneous cuts to public contracts and private incomes. Maintaining repairs protects jobs and school services. The projected deficit is US$7 billion, not the value of the export loss. Fund assets finance a deficit; they do not restore ongoing tax revenue.

Imported equipment means some support raises overseas output. A drawdown has an opportunity cost and can deplete assets if the price fall persists. Continuing every low-value project may displace a training programme that reduces longer-term dependence. Training alone offers little immediate relief where vacancies are distant.

Protect high-value maintenance temporarily if the fund is liquid and the shock likely cyclical. Publish a drawdown rule and reassess the sustainable budget if copper income remains low. Evidence on the fund balance, future prices and local employment would change the recommended scale.

Illustrative domestic purchasing shares are 72% for repairs, 28% for new haul trucks and 86% for training. A larger domestic share limits initial import leakage but does not establish which project creates most benefit.

Best fit, 0–15. 0: no relevant economics. 1–3: assertions or isolated concepts. 4–6: some relevant explanation, limited application. 7–9: coherent analysis with some application and consideration of consequences. 10–12: developed, applied analysis weighing competing considerations with a supported view. 13–15: precise theory and relevant diagrams where useful, evidence integrated throughout, and a balanced judgement that explains conditions or relative importance. Other defensible conclusions can receive full credit.
